# RFC-0003: Result fidelity: previews, committed runs, determinism

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @wael
> **Tags:** `architecture`, `performance`, `out-of-core`

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0003:C-OVERVIEW] Overview and scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0003c-overview"></a>

The same document graph is evaluated for a viewport that needs an answer this frame and for a result a
forester delivers to a client. Those two need different guarantees, and conflating them is how a
camera-dependent number reaches a report.

**Scope** — the two independent ways an evaluation may be reduced; what a preview may and may not be
used for; what reproducibility a committed run guarantees; and when partitioning may adapt to how a
user is working.

**Out of scope** — the operator model and the memory ceiling ([RFC-0002](../rfc/RFC-0002.md)). Camera and viewport
behaviour, and the render synchronisation boundary ([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract)). Which operators exist.

Much of the ground is held before this RFC starts. Level of detail is a stage property the planner can
see ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 4), render state is derived and never authoritative
([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract) 1), and any result diverging from the whole-dataset full-resolution answer must
already declare itself approximate ([RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx)). So a camera cannot change a result, and a
preview is already obliged to admit what it is. What remains is to separate the two reductions people
conflate under "preview", and to say what a committed run promises.

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0003:C-RESOLUTION] Reduced evaluation (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-resolution"></a>

"Preview" conflates two reductions that fail in entirely different ways. Reducing **resolution** over the
full extent yields a noisier version of the right answer, degrading smoothly. Restricting **extent** yields
an answer that is exact inside the region and structurally wrong outside it — a global reduce then
summarises a subset, and a restricted extent has no halo at its boundary, so every neighbourhood operator
is wrong exactly where the user is looking.

1. An evaluation MUST declare its reductions separately:
   - its **resolution floor** — the coarsest level of detail it may draw from;
   - its **extent** — the region it covers.
   - The resolution floor MUST NOT be inferred from the extent, and the extent MUST NOT be inferred from
     the resolution floor.
2. An evaluation MAY be restricted to less than the full extent only if every operator in the pipeline
   declares zero halo width and a single pass ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1).
   - Otherwise it MUST cover the full extent of its input, at whatever resolution floor applies.
3. An evaluation reduced in either respect MUST declare its output approximate under
   [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1.
   - The declared kind of divergence MUST distinguish reduced resolution from restricted extent, and MUST
     name both where both apply.

#### Rationale

(2) is derived rather than invented: the declarations required by [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 already carry
exactly the information needed to decide it. An operator with zero halo and one pass is
position-independent, so restricting its extent is not an approximation at all — cropping, attribute
filtering and reprojection are exact over any subregion. An operator with a halo has no neighbours beyond
the boundary, and a two-pass operator's summary would be built from a subset; in both cases restriction
changes the answer rather than merely reducing it.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly, because the cheap implementation is the wrong one.
Clipping to the visible region is the obvious way to make a preview fast, and for a ground classifier it
produces a hard artefact along the edge of the view that *moves as the camera moves*. A user reads that as
a defect in the software, not as a limitation of previewing — and they are close to right, because nothing
warned them.

(3) supplies the taxonomy that [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1 requires a kind to be drawn from. The two kinds are
not interchangeable: reduced resolution is noise a user can reason about and compensate for, while
restricted extent is a localised error at a known place that must not be trusted at all.

### [RFC-0003:C-PREVIEW] Preview evaluation (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-preview"></a>

A preview exists to answer "does this look roughly right" in a second, not to produce a number anyone
keeps. Its guarantees are correspondingly weak, and the weakness is licensed only because it is already
declared approximate under C-RESOLUTION 3.

1. A preview MUST NOT be used as, or reused to produce, the output of a committed run (C-COMMIT).
   - A committed run MUST re-evaluate rather than consume preview results.
2. A preview is not required to be reproducible.
   - Repeated evaluation of the same graph over the same sources MAY yield differing results within the
     tolerance of its declared reductions.
3. For an unchanged document, unchanged sources and an unchanged camera, successive previews MUST select
   the same resolution floor and the same partition set.
   - Within that, differing reduction order is permitted by (2).
4. A preview MUST NOT be written to a delivered artefact, and any export path MUST route through C-COMMIT.

#### Rationale

(1) and (4) close the failure this clause exists for. A user previews height above ground, the viewport
looks correct, and they export — if the export path can consume what the preview produced, a
camera-dependent, resolution-dependent number has just been delivered as a result. Requiring re-evaluation
makes reuse impossible rather than merely discouraged, which matters because reusing a warm result is
exactly the optimisation someone will reach for.

(2) is the relaxation, and it needs no new disclosure machinery: a preview is already declared approximate,
so non-determinism falls inside a limitation the user has been told about. This is what lets a preview fold
partial reductions as they arrive and take whatever ordering the scheduler finds fastest — the freedom
C-COMMIT gives up.

(3) bounds that relaxation where it would otherwise be felt as a defect, and is stated as an obligation
about *inputs to the evaluation* rather than about what the user perceives, because perception is not
testable. Selecting the same resolution floor and partition set is checkable, and it is what prevents the
visible symptom — points changing colour between frames, or a statistics panel whose digits churn while
nothing moves. Numerical drift within a fixed partition set is below the threshold of a rendered frame.

### [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT] Committed runs (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-commit"></a>

A committed run produces what a forester delivers and may be billed against. [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance)
exists so such an output can be defended to a third party, and a trail that replays to a slightly
different number does not do that job. Determinism is what makes the provenance guarantee mean something.

1. A committed run MUST evaluate at full resolution over its declared extent, and MUST NOT be reduced in
   either respect (C-RESOLUTION 1).
2. A committed run MUST be **bit-identical** across repetitions, given:
   - the same document graph;
   - the same source version fingerprints ([RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding));
   - the same recorded evaluation configuration.
3. Reductions within a committed run MUST combine in a fixed total order derived from partition identity.
   - They MUST NOT combine in order of completion.
   - A reduction accumulated in an associative form under (5) is exempt from this item, and from this item
     alone. It remains bound by (8).
4. The evaluation configuration a committed run used MUST be recorded with its output.
   - The record MUST include the partition size and any other parameter affecting reduction order.
   - It MUST include the identity and version of every transformation backend consulted
     ([RFC-0005:C-BACKEND](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-backend) 4).
   - It MUST include the origin and verification status of every operator evaluated
     ([RFC-0002:C-ORIGIN](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-origin) 2).
5. A reduction within a committed run MUST accumulate in an **associative form**, rather than in floating
   point, where its attribute admits one.
   - An attribute **admits an associative form** where a single quantum distinguishes the smallest value the
     reduction must resolve while the largest total it can reach remains inside the accumulator's range.
   - The three quantities that decide it MUST be declared: the smallest value the reduction must resolve,
     the largest total it can reach, and the range of the accumulator used. An implementation MUST NOT
     narrow the accumulator so as to make an attribute fail the test.
   - A reduction that does not accumulate in an associative form MUST declare that its attribute admits
     none, citing those three quantities. Declaring the refusal is required whether or not any associative
     accumulator has been implemented.
   - A reduction accumulated in an associative form MAY be evaluated by a component that combines partial
     results in an order this specification does not control.
   - A reduction whose attribute admits no associative form MUST combine in the order (3) requires.
6. Conformance to (2) MUST be verified by executing the same committed run twice against the same sources
   and configuration and comparing outputs for bitwise equality.
7. A reduction accumulated under (5) MUST declare its **accumulation quantum** — the step to which an input
   value is rounded before it is accumulated.
   - The quantum MUST be reported alongside the reduction's result value, and a consumer holding that
     output alone MUST be able to read it there.
   - The quantum MUST be expressed as the step itself in the attribute's own unit, and MUST NOT be
     expressed as an exponent, a digit count, or a factor applied to the value.
   - The declaration MUST state a bound on the reduction's departure from an accumulation of the same
     inputs in exact arithmetic. The bound MUST be a stated function of the number of values accumulated
     and of the quantum, and MUST NOT be a function of the partition size or the degree of parallelism.
   - A reduction MUST NOT declare its output approximate ([RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1) on account of its
     quantum alone. A quantum states the resolution at which inputs were distinguished; it is not a
     divergence of the kind C-RESOLUTION 3 enumerates.
   - The quantum MUST be carried as metadata on the field of the reduction's own result. Carrying it only as
     metadata of the batch as a whole MUST NOT be treated as satisfying this: a quantum is per attribute, and
     an operation combining attributes of differing quanta has one batch and several answers.
   - Where a later operation consumes that result and produces a different quantity, the declared quantum
     MUST NOT be presented as applying to the new quantity. Where that operation is delegated, the stage that
     delegates it MUST either declare a quantum for the new quantity or present it without one.
8. A committed reduction's result MUST NOT depend on the degree of parallelism, the number of threads
   available, or the partition size.
   - This binds a reduction reaching the property by either route — the fixed order of (3) or the
     associative form of (5).
9. Conformance to (8), and to the bound declared under (7), MUST be verified by computing the same
   reduction at no fewer than three distinct degrees of parallelism and no fewer than two distinct
   partition sizes, comparing every result for bitwise equality, and confirming that the measured
   departure from exact arithmetic lies within the declared bound.
10. Every attribute over which a reduction may be accumulated under (5) MUST carry the step at which its own
    values are represented, as metadata on its field.
    - For an attribute a stage passes through unchanged ([RFC-0002:C-MATERIALISATION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-materialisation) 1), that step MUST be
      the one the attribute already carries, and MUST NOT be declared finer than the step at which its source
      represents it.
    - A stage that derives an attribute, or that requantises one, MUST declare the step of the attribute it
      produces. It MUST NOT be left to configuration where a source or a deriving stage already determines it.
    - Where the values to be accumulated are produced by an expression evaluated outside Strider, their step
      MUST be declared by the stage that delegates the expression. Reading it from the result MUST NOT be
      relied upon.

#### Rationale

(3) says *partition identity* rather than naming an order because the order is already implied: partitions
are identified by spatial index node keys, so a Morton ordering over those keys is a fixed total order the
system possesses without inventing a sequencing concept. What the obligation costs — partial results cannot
be folded as they land, so a bounded window must be buffered — is the reason it is stated as a MUST rather
than left to implementations.

(8) carries the invariant and (3) and (5) are two means to it, which is why the exemption in (3) is written
as narrowly as it is. An exemption from ordering that also released a reduction from thread-independence
would leave the promise resting on (2) alone — and (2) is conditioned on "the same recorded evaluation
configuration", into which (4) folds every parameter affecting reduction order. That would reduce the
guarantee to identity at one fixed degree of parallelism, which is not what a delivered figure needs.
Stating the invariant separately also gives (9) a proposition to check: bitwise agreement across degrees of
parallelism is evidence for (8), not for the mechanism (5) prescribes.

(5)'s third and fourth bullets are what keep its gate honest. The gate turns on quantities the
implementation chooses, so an implementation could narrow its accumulator until no attribute qualified and
remain conformant on a reading of the first bullet alone; requiring the quantities to be declared, and
forbidding that narrowing, closes it. Requiring the *refusal* to be declared is what makes the obligation
implementable before any associative accumulator exists — a young implementation can be honest about which
attributes it has not handled, which is more useful than silence.

(5)'s fifth bullet is why the clause admits two mechanisms at all. A fixed reduction order is enforceable
only where this specification controls the scheduler, and a general-purpose analytical engine combines
partial results as they arrive. Why accumulating differently is preferable to constraining such an engine is
a comparative question, argued in the accompanying architecture decision rather than here.

(7) exists because (5) exchanges one guarantee for another and the exchange has to be visible. An
associative accumulation is exactly reproducible at its quantum and is *not* the most accurate sum
available: values are rounded before they are accumulated. Requiring the quantum beside the value, rather
than in (4)'s record alone, is what lets a third party check a delivered figure without holding the run's
configuration — the reader [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) exists to serve.

The term is **quantum** and not *scale* deliberately. In fixed-point and decimal representations "scale"
already names a digit count, and a reader who knows that reads a declared scale as evidence that the stored
value has been multiplied — which is the one thing (7) is not saying. Nothing in a result is scaled: what is
reported is a step size in the attribute's own unit, beside a value in that same unit. *Quantisation*
remains the name of the process, as [RFC-0005:C-TRANSFORM](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-transform) already uses it.

(7)'s bullet on approximation settles a question two clauses would otherwise leave open.
[RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1 is triggered by a result differing from its whole-dataset, full-resolution
formulation, and a quantised total does differ from an unrounded one — so on a literal reading every
committed reduction would owe an approximate declaration, while (1) simultaneously promises full resolution
and C-RESOLUTION 3's enumeration of reduced evaluations
offers no kind to name. Treating a quantum as measurement resolution rather than divergence resolves it in
the direction that keeps both clauses meaningful: an instrument's precision does not make a measurement an
approximation of itself.

(5)'s availability is wider than it looks, which is why the obligation is not onerous: LAS and COPC store
coordinates as scaled integers, so positional attributes almost always admit an associative form.

(10) answers *where a step comes from*, and the answer is mostly that it is not chosen. The same fact that
makes (5) widely available supplies it: a source storing coordinates as scaled integers has already fixed the
finest step at which it distinguishes them, so for a passed-through attribute the step is a property of the
input, not a setting. Declaring one *finer* than that is the specific error worth prohibiting, because it
claims a resolution the data never had, and the bound (7) requires would then be truthful about the
arithmetic and wrong about the measurement. Declaring a coarser one is permitted and sometimes forced — a
stage that requantises produces genuinely coarser values, which is why that stage declares the new figure
rather than inheriting the old.

(10) is a separate item from (7) because it has a different subject. (7) binds a *reduction*; a stage that
passes an attribute through, or derives one, may perform no reduction at all, so bullets about such stages
did not belong under a head that speaks only of reductions. Reading them there left it undecidable whether a
stage that reduces nothing owed anything.

Exposing a step to configuration was the alternative and it is worse for a reason that generalises: a
correctness-relevant quantity decidable by someone with no way to know the answer, whose failure mode is a
bound that reads as authoritative. Making it a declaration by the party that determines the values puts it
under (5)'s regime with everything else.

Field metadata is the carrier for the reason measured for coordinate reference systems: a per-attribute fact
stored per batch has one slot, and an operation combining two attributes with different quanta keeps one of
them without saying which. Measured, a quantum attached to a reduction's own result field survived aliasing,
grouping, sub-queries and joins.

It did **not** survive one shape, and (7)'s last bullet is that finding rather than a hypothetical: where an
expression consumes a reduction's result, the engine builds a fresh field and the quantum does not travel.
That loss is arguably correct rather than a defect — twice a total is a different quantity, whose precision is
not the reduction's — but it means the tag cannot be read as blanket provenance. It states something about an
*unmodified* result. So the obligation is not that the tag must somehow survive; it is that a quantity derived
from a reduction must not be presented as carrying the reduction's quantum. (10)'s last bullet is the same
finding from the input side: where the values accumulated are themselves produced by a delegated expression,
the step has to be declared by whoever delegated it, because the result's field will not carry one.

(9) complements (6) rather than replacing it, and the two catch different implementations. A reduction that
merges partials as they arrive is usually unstable from one run to the next, so (6) catches it. What (6)
cannot catch is a reduction that has been made stable *within* a configuration — by pinning a thread pool,
or by fixing an order within each partition but not across them — while still answering differently at a
different degree of parallelism or partition size. Nothing in (6) varies either, so nothing in (6) looks.
Three distinct degrees is the smallest number that distinguishes a stable result from two that happen to
agree; two partition sizes is what makes the cross-configuration half of (8) checkable rather than merely
claimed.

### [RFC-0003:C-PARTITIONING] Adaptive partitioning (Normative) <a id="rfc-0003c-partitioning"></a>

A cache that reshapes partitions to match how a user is working is a real optimisation — merging nodes
while the camera orbits one tree, subdividing them for finer working sets. It is also incompatible with
bit-identical results, because partition identity is what fixes reduction order. So it is permitted exactly
where nothing reproducible depends on it, and desirable there.

1. Partitioning used for a committed run MUST be derived only from the source's spatial index and the
   operators' declared requirements.
   - It MUST NOT depend on interaction history, cache state, or camera position.
   - An adapted partitioning MUST NOT be reused for a committed run, including where one is already
     resident.
2. Partitioning used for preview or rendering MAY adapt to access patterns, merging or subdividing freely.
3. A cache MUST NOT subdivide a partition in order to satisfy an operator's neighbourhood requirement.
   - Supplying neighbours is the planner's duty, discharged from the declared halo width
     ([RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 and [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3).
4. A partitioning MAY be established in a frame related to the source's frame by an isometry.
   - The isometry MUST be recorded as part of the coordinate reference system the resulting coordinates
     carry ([RFC-0005:C-CRS](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-crs) 1). Leaving it implicit MUST NOT be treated as satisfying this.
   - One frame SHOULD serve a whole partitioning rather than a separate frame per partition.

#### Rationale

(1) is entailed by C-COMMIT 3, C-COMMIT 4 and [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) 5 taken together — reduction order
fixed by partition identity, a recorded partition size, and a fingerprint on every derived artefact. An
adaptive partitioning satisfies none of the three. The nested prohibition on *reuse* is stated separately
because entailment does not stop an already-warm adapted partitioning from being picked up, which is the
concrete way this is violated in practice.

(2) is not merely tolerated but wanted, and it is licensed by the same split that governs everything else:
render state is derived and never authoritative ([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract) 1 and 2), and previews are already
released from reproducibility by C-PREVIEW 2. Nothing repeatable depends on the shape of a render
partition, so the cache may do whatever serves the interaction.

(3) is stated as a prohibition on the *cache* rather than as a restatement of the planner's duty, which
[RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) already owns. The point is that a second, non-deterministic mechanism for supplying
neighbours must not appear alongside the deterministic one.

(4) is a permission rather than a requirement, and it is worth stating because the thing it permits is easy
to reach for badly. A survey strip running diagonally across the source's axes fills an axis-aligned tiling
with mostly-empty partitions, and empty partitions are not merely wasteful: halo cost scales with boundary
area, and an ill-fitting tiling is precisely what maximises boundary area per point. Establishing the
partitioning in a frame that fits the data addresses both at once.

It is an isometry specifically because that is the class [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 already shows preserves
everything a partitioning depends on — distances, so declared halo widths stay widths; containment, so
membership is unchanged; and partition identity, so the reduction order C-COMMIT 3 derives from spatial index
keys is untouched. Nothing further needs saying about safety.

The recording obligation is the only MUST here because it is the only part with a silent failure. Coordinates
in an unrecorded frame are indistinguishable from coordinates in the source's frame, so every consumer places
the data confidently in the wrong location — the same hazard [RFC-0005:C-CRS](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-crs) 3 refuses for an absent
system, arriving by a different route. Recording it in the coordinate reference system is also what keeps
(1) satisfied for a committed run: once the frame is part of how the coordinates are described, choosing it
is not a runtime adaptation, even where the rotation was originally derived from the data.

One frame per partitioning is a SHOULD and not a MUST because the literature does the other thing and may be
right for cases this project has not measured. Orienting *each node* by principal component analysis is an
established technique and reports tighter volumes than a single rotation. What it costs is the global
lattice: node keys computed from coordinates presume one frame, and a halo crosses partition boundaries by
construction, so per-partition frames make a halo's points arrive in a different frame from the core points
they serve, and leave the grid-alignment reasoning in [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 without a common grid to reason
about. Those are strong reasons for one frame and not proofs that per-partition frames cannot be made to
work, so the clause advises rather than forbids.

Nothing here constrains the *shape* of a partition's bounds. [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 4 requires bounds to be
declared and says nothing about their orientation, and [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 is deliberately written in terms
of properties an alteration must preserve rather than transformations it may apply. An implementation that
finds oriented bounds worth the cost is not obstructed; it is simply not the arrangement this clause makes
cheapest.
